newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers raise stakes after talks fail.
newsitem.headline: French truckers raise stakes after talks fail.

text.p: French truckers' unions stepped up pressure on the government on Friday after talks with haulage bosses broke down, blockading roads for a fifth day and sealing off more petrol depots around the country.

Wary of a conflict reminiscent of last year's crippling 24-day rail strike, the government bowed to a demand from the truckers unions, agreeing to send a Transport Ministry official to the next round of talks due to start at 1800 GMT, unions and officials said.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe had earlier appeared to reject demands that the government participate in the talks and agree to co-finance retirement at 55 instead of 60 for drivers.

"We are aware of the importance of this economic sector for the country and the negotiations must restart quickly and lead to a solution," Juppe said in Bordeaux, the southwestern city where he serves as mayor.
"A solution must be found through talks between haulage bosses and their employees," he said.
Truckers have singled out Bordeaux as the main focus of protests, causing huge traffic jams on all access roads. Airlines at Bordeaux airport said air freight was badly hit.
For the first time in five days, truckers formed blockades for about an hour on access roads to Paris after union representatives broke off the negotiations in the small hours.

Lorries blocked the A86 motorway at the Nogent Bridge east of the capital and other trucks crawled along at a snail's pace at another eastern access in Bagnolet. In the Mediterranean port of Marseille, unions urged truckers to make for the capital.
Nicole Notat, leader of France's biggest union, the pro-Socialist CFDT, threatened to call a demonstration in the capital for Monday if talks failed to break the impasse.

"Our disagreement with them is total. We must maintain pressure for things to advance," said Claude Debons of the CFDT truckers union, whose members are demanding wage rises, shorter working hours and retirement at 55.
About 50,000 trucks were taking part in the protests according to unions, and the drivers were bent on continuing their action until their demands were met.

Truckers blockaded a dozen petrol depots and refineries, threatening a supply shortage soon. Lorries blocked the Lille-Paris motorway near Lille and 15 lorries prevented tanks at the Donges refinery near Saint-Nazaire from being filled.

After blockading depots in Bordeaux and Caen, lorries also sealed off depots in Lyon, Fos-sur-Mer, Lacq and Frontignan. Two other refineries in the Bouches-du-Rhone and the Marseille region were also closed off.

Motorways in and out of 30 towns and cities across the country were blocked by trucks, recalling a 1992 truckers' blockade that paralysed France in a protest against a new points system for driving licences.
Toulouse, Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, Caen, Le Mans and the Franco-German border at Strasbourg were among the hardest hit.

Unions said earlier they might blockade the capital but only as a last resort. "Blockades are more efficient 150 kms away (90 miles) from Paris rather than just around the city," said one official who took part in the negotiations.
The government is wary of taking a soft stance as several big companies including car-makers Renault and PSA Peugeot Citroen want its approval for plans to lay off workers at 55.
Brigitte Bardot, film goddess turned animal rights activist, urged veterinary services to ensure that animals stranded in the trucks in cold weather were fed and given water.
"I respect the truckers' grievances but I ask them not to let the animals, who are at the heart of the conflict, agonise," she said.
